quantity.description: Change in own-team expected single-game scoring margin from adopting the strategy
quantity.support: unbounded real; positive favors own team

prior.consistency_check: 0.5 lies within [-0.3, 1.3]; normal distribution has unbounded signed support, consistent with the quantity definition.

distribution_family.justification: Well-studied domain with fairly symmetric uncertainty around a positive but modest expected gain; no strong reason to expect a long one-sided tail.
distribution_family.name: normal

strategies.rationale: Decades of research (Romer, Burke, nflfastR models) show coaches are systematically too conservative; the gap between optimal and actual behavior is largest in the plays coaches still avoid (own territory, 4th-and-medium). Closing this gap adds expected points and wins over a season.
strategies.recommendation: Go for it on 4th-and-short (≤2 yards) from any field position where win-probability models favor it, not just at midfield or in obvious 'analytics-approved' zones (e.g., own 35-45). Extend this to 4th-and-3-4 in opponent territory when expected points favor conversion attempts over field goals/punts.
strategies.title: Expand 4th-down go-for-it range

prior.consistency_check: 0.4 lies within [-0.4, 1.2]; normal family covers all signed real values as required.

distribution_family.justification: Effect is directionally well-supported but roster-dependent (O-line, QB, WR talent), giving a roughly symmetric band of uncertainty around a modest positive mean.
distribution_family.name: normal

strategies.rationale: Public EPA/success-rate models consistently show early-down passing outperforms early-down running for most rosters, yet league-wide run rates on 1st/2nd down remain higher than optimal; capturing more of this gap improves per-drive scoring efficiency.
strategies.recommendation: Increase first- and second-down dropback rate (including play-action from run-heavy sets) toward the EPA-optimal mix identified in public models, rather than defaulting to early-down runs to 'set up' later downs.
strategies.title: Raise early-down pass rate

prior.consistency_check: 0.3 lies within [-0.5, 1.1]; normal family supports all signed real values.

distribution_family.justification: Effect depends on secondary talent and defensive line's ability to still generate pressure from two-high looks; uncertainty is fairly balanced around a small positive mean.
distribution_family.name: normal

strategies.rationale: Public tracking-data research links single-high shells to higher explosive-pass-play rates, and explosive plays are disproportionately correlated with win probability swings; reducing them via two-high shells lowers opponent EPA/play even if it concedes slightly more underneath completions.
strategies.recommendation: Shift base early-down defense toward two-high shells (Cover 2/4/6 variants with post-snap rotation) instead of single-high (Cover 1/3), reserving single-high for clear passing downs or specific personnel matchups.
strategies.title: More two-high (split safety) shells on early downs

prior.consistency_check: 0.05 lies within [-0.55, 0.65]; normal family covers signed values, appropriate given the near-zero, weak-effect honesty required here.

distribution_family.justification: This is a low-leverage, low-confidence effect; a tight, symmetric, light-tailed distribution near zero reflects genuine near-indifference rather than a strong directional belief.
distribution_family.name: normal

strategies.rationale: Public research on icing the kicker is genuinely mixed/inconclusive (some studies show no effect, a few show a small negative effect for the icing team via rhythm/rest benefits to the kicker); this is not settled analytics, so the call rests on my own read that the timeout is more valuable held in reserve than spent trying to rattle a kicker who has already had a full week to prepare for pressure kicks.
strategies.recommendation: Eliminate the pre-kick 'icing' timeout before opponent field-goal attempts; instead, save that timeout for offensive/defensive use later in the possession or half.
strategies.title: Stop icing the opposing kicker

prior.consistency_check: Mode ≈ -0.17 + 1.11*0.422 ≈ 0.30, inside [-0.9, 1.9]; skew-normal has unbounded signed support satisfying the quantity definition.

distribution_family.justification: Upside (a scouted gadget play breaking for an explosive gain) is larger in magnitude than the bounded downside (a stuffed/failed trick play), producing a genuinely asymmetric belief that a symmetric family cannot represent.
distribution_family.name: skew_normal

parameters.conversion_note: Fit numerically: for alpha=4, delta=alpha/sqrt(1+alpha^2)=0.970; standardized mode ≈0.422, mean ≈0.774, sd≈0.633 (via Azzalini skew-normal formulas). Solving mode_actual = xi + omega*0.422 = 0.3 and setting omega ≈ (95%-range)/4 = 2.8/4 = 0.7/0.633 = 1.106 (rounded 1.11) gives xi = 0.3 - 0.422*1.11 ≈ -0.17. Approximate values, fit to match qualitative mode and spread rather than exact percentile solving.

strategies.rationale: This is not something aggregate EPA models can evaluate well — sample sizes per unique play/opponent pairing are tiny and success hinges on qualitative scouting reads (a specific defender's eye discipline, a specific coordinator's tendency) that don't show up in league-wide play-type data. My own experience is that a well-timed, well-scouted gadget play produces disproportionate explosive-play value, but a poorly-timed one costs field position or turnovers.
strategies.recommendation: Install one or two bespoke gadget plays (wildcat, unbalanced line, jet-sweep motion misdirection) each week targeted at a specific leverage or discipline weakness scouted on film for that opponent, rather than running generic change-of-pace plays from a standing library.
strategies.title: Opponent-specific gadget/formation packages

prior.consistency_check: 0.25 lies within [-0.75, 1.25]; Student-t distribution has unbounded signed support, consistent with the quantity's definition and the heavier-tail belief.

distribution_family.justification: This effect depends on subjective, hard-to-repeat in-game judgment; there's a non-trivial chance of a large effect in either direction (a well-timed blitz forcing a game-changing turnover, or a badly-timed one giving up an explosive play), warranting heavier tails than a normal distribution.
distribution_family.name: student_t

strategies.rationale: Public blitz-rate analytics is mixed/near-neutral in aggregate (blitzing doesn't clearly raise defensive EPA on average), which masks the fact that the *value* of pressure is highly QB-state-dependent — something no dataset captures well since it requires real-time qualitative judgment rather than pre-game tendencies. My own read across games is that pressure timed to visible QB discomfort outperforms pressure called by formula.
strategies.recommendation: Dial up Cover-0/all-out pressure looks not on a fixed down-and-distance script, but triggered live by a coach's read of quarterback stress cues (rushed cadence, frequent pre-snap motion checks, visible discomfort against prior pressure) — especially against backup or rattled starting QBs.
strategies.title: Real-time-read situational all-out pressure
